messages.body: Hello Lan — welcome. We are the Hangyul Univ team working on your applications to Pusan National University and Kyungpook National University. You can ask us anything here.
Hello! Thank you. I uploaded my passport, photo, diploma and TOPIK certificate yesterday.
All four are verified. Your transcript still needs an apostille — the copy you uploaded is not authenticated yet. The steps are on the Documents page.
I went to the Consular Department this morning. They said five working days.
That fits the Kyungpook deadline. Please upload it as soon as you have it and we will check it the same day.

Thank you! One more question about the bank certificate: my father's account is in VND and the balance changes every week because of his business. Should the certificate show the balance on one day, or the average over three months? The bank in Hải Phòng says they can issue either one, but the three-month version takes five working days and costs more. I also want to ask whether the translation has to be done by a certified office in Hà Nội, or whether the university accepts a translation certified by the bank itself. I can send photos of both sample forms if that helps.

A balance certificate for one day is enough for both universities — it must be issued within 30 days of the application. A translation certified by the bank is accepted. No need for the three-month version.
I left comments on your personal statement. Your story about translating snack labels is great — let's make the project result more concrete.

body.title: Personal statement — Pusan National University

findings.text: 168 words of 1000 — there is room to say more about your goals.

body.body:
When I was sixteen, my aunt opened a small shop in Hải Phòng that sold Korean snacks. None of the labels were in Vietnamese, so every weekend I sat behind the counter with a dictionary and translated them one by one. Customers started asking me what was inside each package, and I realised that a product only becomes real to people when someone explains it in their own language.

That shop is why I want to study business in Korea. In high school I led a project that compared how three Korean brands advertise in Viet Nam. We interviewed customers and presented our results at the school fair. The project taught me how to ask questions and how to listen to the answers.

I have studied Korean for three years and passed TOPIK level 4. At university I want to learn marketing strategy and consumer research, and after graduation I hope to work between Korean and Vietnamese companies so that more small shops like my aunt's can grow.

body.body:
In my first year I will focus on the Korean language and on the foundation courses of the business school: principles of management, economics and statistics. I plan to reach TOPIK level 5 before the second year.

From the second year I want to take marketing, consumer behaviour and international business. I also plan to join a student club that works with local companies.

body.body:
When I was sixteen, my aunt opened a small shop in Hải Phòng that sold Korean snacks. None of the labels were in Vietnamese, so every weekend I sat behind the counter with a dictionary and translated them one by one. Customers started asking me what was inside each package, and I realised that a product only becomes real to people when someone explains it in their own language.

That shop is why I want to study business in Korea. In high school I led a project that compared how three Korean brands advertise in Viet Nam. We interviewed customers and presented our results at the school fair. The project taught me how to ask questions and how to listen to the answers.

I have studied Korean for three years and passed TOPIK level 4. At university I want to learn marketing strategy and consumer research, and after graduation I hope to work between Korean and Vietnamese companies so that more small shops like my aunt's can grow.
